key_terms.meaning: A circuit that can be drawn on a flat sheet with no branch crossing another branch.
A closed loop that contains no other loop inside it; mesh current flows around it clockwise.
Two meshes joined into one path by removing the shared current source; gives one KVL equation plus one constraint i₂ − i₁ = I.
The voltage of a node measured with respect to the chosen reference node (0 V).
The one node fixed at 0 V, usually the bottom or most-connected node; every other voltage is written relative to it.
Two nodes joined into one by enclosing the voltage source between them; gives one KCL equation plus one constraint V_a − V_b = V.
A circuit is linear if it obeys both additivity and homogeneity of its response with respect to its sources.
Total response = sum of responses to each independent source acting alone, with other independent sources set to zero.
Replacing V in series with R by I = V/R in parallel with R, or the reverse; the terminal behaviour stays the same.
The open-circuit voltage seen at the two terminals of the network.
The resistance looking into the terminals with all independent sources set to zero; equals V_oc/I_sc.
The short-circuit current at the terminals; I_N = V_th/R_th and R_N = R_th.
A fixed source gives maximum load power when R_L = R_th, and P_max = V_th²/(4R_th).
In a linear bilateral network, swapping the source branch and the response branch leaves the current ratio unchanged: I₂/V₁ = I₁/V₂.
Parallel branches of (V_k, R_k) reduce to one source V = Σ(V_k/R_k) ÷ Σ(1/R_k) in series with R = 1 ÷ Σ(1/R_k).
For any network satisfying KCL and KVL, Σ v_k i_k = 0 over all elements, with each product taken in the passive sign convention.
Maximum power in the phasor domain needs Z_L = Z_th* (same resistance, opposite reactance).
V_th and Z_th = R_th + jX_th found with complex impedances at one fixed frequency, with sources set to zero as before.

takeaways: Mesh analysis writes KVL around each mesh and solves for mesh currents; a shared current source becomes one supermesh equation plus a current constraint.
Nodal analysis writes KCL at each non-reference node and solves for node voltages; a floating voltage source becomes one supernode equation plus a voltage constraint.
Superposition applies only to linear circuits, and only to voltages and currents, never directly to power.
Any linear two-terminal network reduces to a single source and a single resistance, which makes load calculations one-step.
A source delivers maximum power to a load when the load resistance equals the source resistance, but the efficiency then is only 50 per cent.
Reciprocity, Millman and Tellegen give fast checks on a solution without re-solving the whole circuit.
In AC circuits, every theorem survives if resistance is replaced by impedance and numbers become phasors at one frequency.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit almost always ask for a full worked circuit: state the law used, number the meshes or nodes on a diagram, solve the simultaneous equations, and close with a verification step such as Tellegen's sum or a power balance.

bank.q: Define a mesh and a node. List, in order, the steps of mesh analysis for a planar DC circuit containing only voltage sources, and explain why a current source needs special handling.
outline: Mesh = innermost closed loop; node = junction of two or more elements.
Assign clockwise mesh currents i₁, i₂, …
Write KVL per mesh: sum of resistance drops minus shared drops = sum of source emfs.
Current source inside one mesh fixes that mesh current directly.
Current source shared by two meshes needs a supermesh plus a constraint equation.

bank.q: State the superposition theorem. Explain what 'setting an independent source to zero' means for an ideal voltage source and for an ideal current source, and why power cannot be found by superposition.
outline: Statement: total response = algebraic sum of responses to each independent source acting alone.
Zero voltage source = short circuit (0 V).
Zero current source = open circuit (0 A).
Only one independent source active at a time; dependent sources stay in place.
Power is proportional to current squared or voltage squared, so it is not linear.
Powers of individual responses are not added.

bank.q: State Thevenin's theorem and Norton's theorem. Give the relations between V_th, I_N, R_th and R_N, and state how R_th is measured when dependent sources are present.
outline: Thevenin: V_th in series with R_th.
Norton: I_N in parallel with R_N.
R_N = R_th; I_N = V_th/R_th; V_th = I_N R_N.
R_th = V_oc/I_sc at the terminals.
With dependent sources, V_oc and I_sc must be measured; cannot simply kill all sources.

bank.q: State the maximum power transfer theorem for a DC source and derive the condition R_L = R_th with the value P_max = V_th²/(4R_th). State the efficiency at that point.
outline: P_L = i²R_L with i = V_th/(R_th + R_L).
P_L = V_th²R_L/(R_th + R_L)².
Differentiate with respect to R_L and set to zero.
(R_th + R_L)² − 2R_L(R_th + R_L) = 0 → R_L = R_th.
P_max = V_th²/(4R_th).
Efficiency = P_L/P_generated = 50 per cent.

bank.q: A planar DC network has three meshes; a 4 A current source is shared between meshes 2 and 3. Write the mesh equations including the supermesh equation, and solve for all three mesh currents.
outline: Draw and label the three clockwise mesh currents.
Write KVL for meshes 1 and 3 in full.
Combine meshes 2 and 3 into one supermesh; write KVL around the outer path of the supermesh.
Constraint from the shared source: i₃ − i₂ = 4 (sign from assigned directions).
Solve the three simultaneous equations.
Check by substituting into an unused KVL around an outer loop.

bank.q: For a circuit with four nodes and a 12 V source connected directly between two non-reference nodes, write the nodal equations using a supernode and find all node voltages.
outline: Mark the reference node and label V_a, V_b, V_c.
Write KCL at ordinary nodes in the form (V − V_neighbour)/R.
Enclose the 12 V source in a supernode; write one KCL for the supernode.
Constraint: V_a − V_b = 12 V.
Solve the simultaneous equations.
Check that KCL is satisfied at the reference node.

bank.q: A resistive circuit has a 10 V voltage source and a 2 A current source. Use superposition to find the current through a specified 5 Ω resistor, then compute the power in it and explain why the power is not the sum of the two partial powers.
outline: Kill the current source (open) and solve for I'.
Kill the voltage source (short) and solve for I''.
Add with signs: I = I' + I''.
P = I²R using the total current.
I'²R + I''²R ≠ (I' + I'')²R because of the cross term 2I'I''R.
Power is a nonlinear (squared) quantity.

bank.q: Find the Thevenin equivalent of a two-terminal network that contains one dependent source and two independent sources, then use it to find the current in a 6 Ω load.
outline: Remove the load; find V_oc by any method (nodal or mesh).
Find I_sc by shorting the terminals.
R_th = V_oc/I_sc; dependent sources stay in place.
Draw the Thevenin circuit: V_th in series with R_th.
I_L = V_th/(R_th + 6).
Note that killing the dependent source is wrong.

bank.q: Three parallel branches hold 10 V with 2 Ω, 6 V with 3 Ω, and 4 V with 6 Ω. Use Millman's theorem to find the common node voltage and the current in each branch.
outline: V = Σ(V_k/R_k)/Σ(1/R_k).
Denominator: 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1 S.
I_k = (V_k − V)/R_k for each branch.
Check ΣI_k = 0 at the node.

bank.q: An AC network with a 50 Hz source has R = 4 Ω in series with L = 10 mH. Find the Thevenin impedance seen by the load, then the load impedance for maximum power transfer.
outline: |Z_th| = 5.09 Ω, angle 38.1 degrees.
Conjugate match: Z_L = 4 − j3.14 Ω.
P_max = |V_th|²/(4R_th), with R_th = 4 Ω.
Reactance is cancelled, so the load looks purely resistive to the source.
Note that equal-impedance (not conjugate) matching wastes power.

bank.q: Compare mesh analysis and nodal analysis for a given planar network. State which method gives fewer equations for a circuit with 6 meshes and 4 non-reference nodes, and justify each choice.
outline: Mesh needs b − n + 1 equations; nodal needs n − 1 equations.
Here 6 mesh equations versus 4 nodal equations, so nodal is shorter.
Mesh suits networks with many parallel branches and few loops.
Current sources suit nodal analysis; voltage sources suit mesh analysis.
Presence of a supernode or supermesh adds one equation but removes one unknown.
Both methods reduce to solving a linear system.

bank.q: A lamp fed from a long cable dims when a heater is switched on. Use Thevenin's theorem to model the cable-plus-supply as a source, and show how the terminal voltage falls with load current.
outline: Supply and cable reduce to V_th in series with R_th.
Terminal voltage V = V_th − I R_th.
Higher load current gives a bigger drop across R_th.
Lamp current falls from its no-load value.
Fault diagnosis: measure V_oc and V_under_load, then R_th = (V_oc − V_load)/I_load.
Choose a thicker cable to reduce R_th.

bank.q: For a given DC circuit, verify Tellegen's theorem by computing Σ v_k i_k over all elements, and explain what the zero sum tells you about power balance.
outline: Solve the circuit for all element voltages and currents.
Use the passive sign convention for every element, including sources.
Sources give negative products; resistors give positive products.
The sum Σ v_k i_k = 0.
Meaning: total power supplied equals total power absorbed.
Any nonzero total signals an arithmetic error.

bank.q: A signal source of 50 Ω internal resistance feeds a load. Discuss when to use the conjugate match and when to use a matched-impedance or low-reflection connection, and compute the power lost in each case.
outline: Conjugate match Z_L = Z_th* maximises load power.
Half the power is lost in R_th at that point.
In power systems, maximum efficiency (R_L much greater than R_th) is preferred over maximum power.
In communication and RF, maximum power matters more than efficiency.
Reflection coefficient Γ = (Z_L − Z_th)/(Z_L + Z_th); Γ = 0 only for a matched-impedance, non-conjugate case.
State the application before choosing the criterion.

glossary.def: A single element or a series of elements carrying the same current between two nodes.
Any closed path in a circuit; a mesh is a loop with no other loop inside it.
A fictitious circulating current assigned to one mesh, used as the unknown in mesh analysis.
The combined outer loop formed by two meshes that share a current source.
A point where two or more circuit elements meet.
The closed surface formed by two nodes joined by a voltage source, treated as one node for KCL.
The node chosen as 0 V so that all other node voltages are measured against it.
Kirchhoff's current law: the algebraic sum of currents leaving a node is zero.
Kirchhoff's voltage law: the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero.
An element whose voltage-current relation is a straight line through the origin, such as an ideal resistor.
Scaling every source by a factor k scales every response by the same k.
The response to a sum of sources equals the sum of the responses to each source alone.
An element that behaves the same when its terminals are swapped, such as a resistor.
The voltage across two terminals when no load is connected.
The current that flows through a zero-ohm link placed across two terminals.
A source whose value is controlled by a voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit; it is never set to zero in superposition.
Swapping a voltage source in series with a resistor for a current source in parallel with the same resistor, or the reverse.
The property that a source in branch 1 and an ammeter in branch 2 give the same reading when their roles are swapped.
A formula that turns several parallel voltage-source branches into one equivalent source and resistance.
Conservation of power in network form: Σ v_k i_k = 0 for every network obeying KCL and KVL, linear or not.
The complex ratio V/I in the phasor domain, written Z = R + jX with R in ohms and X the reactance in ohms.
A complex number representing the amplitude and phase of a sinusoid at one fixed frequency.
Useful output power divided by total power supplied, expressed as a percentage.
The element or network connected to the two output terminals of a source network.
